The Soft Girl's Guide To Becoming A Full-Time YouTube Creator

A free, ebook-length teaching guide to building a YouTube channel from zero: niche, setup, planning, scripting, filming, editing, titles and thumbnails, analytics, every real way to earn, scam warnings and a 7, 30 and 90-day plan. Honest about what full-time really takes.

By Princess Immanuel · Founder, Her Digital Playbook

Come and sit with me, love. Let us talk about YouTube: the place where a woman with a phone, a window and something useful to say can build an audience, a body of work and, for some, a real income.

I want to be gentle and honest at the same time. The title of this guide says "full-time," and that is a real possibility for some creators. But it is not the usual result, and it is almost never fast. Most channels grow slowly. Many earn little for a long time. Some never earn at all. A few build something that replaces a salary, and they usually did it by combining several kinds of income, not by views alone. This guide shows you how that works from zero, so you can decide with open eyes and then build properly.

I will define every word, explain every step and give you scripts, templates, checklists and plans. Nothing is skipped, and nothing is assumed. You do not need to be on camera, loud, technical or "aesthetic" to begin. You need a clear idea, a way to record, patience and a willingness to improve a little with every video.

A few honest promises before we start.

I cannot promise you any views, subscribers, income or dates. Results depend on your niche, skills, consistency, luck, country and timing. Anyone who guarantees you a number of subscribers or a monthly income is selling you something.

I am not a lawyer, tax adviser or financial adviser. Where this guide touches on money, contracts, copyright, taxes and privacy, I am teaching general ideas. Rules differ by country and change over time, so please check what applies to you and speak to a qualified person about anything important.

YouTube changes its features, programmes, eligibility rules, policies and payment terms often. When I mention a feature or requirement, treat it as an example and check YouTube's current help pages and policies before you rely on it.

And I will not tell you that you need an expensive camera, a studio or a perfect face. You do not. Many successful channels began with a phone.

Here is what you will learn:

  • What a YouTube channel is, and how the platform actually decides what to show.
  • Honest expectations: timelines, numbers and what "full-time" really takes.
  • How to choose a niche and understand your viewer.
  • How to set up a channel that looks clear and trustworthy.
  • The tools you need, and the ones you can ignore.
  • How to plan, script, film and edit videos without burning out.
  • How to write titles, thumbnails and hooks that earn clicks honestly.
  • How to read your analytics and improve.
  • Every real way to earn: ads, memberships, affiliate links, sponsorships, your own products and services.
  • Copyright, rules, scams and safety.
  • A seven, thirty and ninety-day plan, plus scripts, a checklist and a one-page plan.
Big Sis Note 💖 You do not have to read this in one go. Take a chapter at a time and do the small task at the end of each. Understanding grows from doing, not from reading faster.

1Meet Your Channel

Let us start with the words, because the platform has its own language.

A channel is your home on YouTube: the page that holds your videos, your name, your description and your subscribers.

A video is a piece of content you upload. A long-form video is a regular video, usually a few minutes or longer. Shorts are very short vertical videos, built to be watched quickly in a vertical feed.

A subscriber is someone who chose to follow your channel. A view is counted when someone watches a video, under rules that YouTube defines.

Watch time is the total amount of time people spend watching your videos. Average view duration is how long people watch on average. Audience retention is a graph showing at what points people stop watching.

Impressions are the number of times your thumbnail was shown to people. Click-through rate, often shortened to CTR, is the percentage of impressions that turned into clicks. If your thumbnail was shown a hundred times and ten people clicked, your click-through rate is ten percent.

A thumbnail is the small image that represents your video. A title is the text above it. Together they decide whether someone clicks.

A hook is the first few seconds of a video, which must give people a reason to keep watching.

The algorithm, in plain words, is the set of systems that decide which videos to show to which people on the home page, in search results and in suggestions. Nobody outside YouTube knows the exact rules, and they change. The best summary is that YouTube tries to show people videos they will click and enjoy.

A niche is a specific topic or group of viewers you serve.

Evergreen content stays useful for a long time. Trend content is tied to a moment and fades quickly.

Monetization means earning money from your channel. The YouTube Partner Programme is YouTube's programme that allows eligible channels to earn from ads and certain features. Eligibility requirements exist, and they have changed over time, so you must check the current rules.

RPM and CPM are measurements of how much money is earned per thousand views or ad views, with different definitions. They vary hugely by niche, country, season and audience. Treat any single number you see online with caution.

A community post is a short update to your subscribers. A playlist is a collection of videos.

Analytics is the data YouTube gives you about your channel and videos.

Copyright is the legal protection that owners have over their work, including music, video clips, images and writing. A copyright claim or strike can affect your videos and channel. Respecting copyright is essential.

Take your time with this list. You can return to it whenever you need.

How YouTube works, in plain words

People find videos in four main ways.

Search. Someone types a question or phrase, and videos appear. Search-driven videos, such as "how to make a monthly budget," can bring viewers for years.

Browse (the home feed). YouTube shows videos it thinks a person might enjoy, based on their history. This is where interest-based and entertaining videos can spread.

Suggested videos. After one video, YouTube recommends others. Being suggested next to a related video can bring steady viewers.

External sources. Links from social media, websites, email and messaging apps.

Understanding these four helps you plan. Search-led content is slower to start and steady over time. Browse-led content can spike and fade. Most beginners do well starting with search-friendly videos that answer clear questions, and adding more creative formats as they learn.

What YouTube is trying to do

YouTube wants viewers to stay on the platform and feel satisfied. Videos that people click and watch for a good length of time, and then watch more, tend to be shown to more people. This means your job is not to trick the algorithm. Your job is to make something that the right viewer clicks, enjoys and finds useful. Honest titles, clear thumbnails, strong hooks and genuinely helpful content do this better than any trick.

A made-up example

Take Adaora, a made-up example. She posts a few tidy, calm videos about simple budget meals for students. Her first ten videos get very few views. She improves her titles, speaks more clearly in the first ten seconds and makes one video answering a question people keep asking: "What can I cook with only rice and eggs?" That video is found through search and keeps getting a few views a day for months. It teaches her what her viewers want, and her next videos build on it. This is a typical pattern: slow, then a small signal, then steady learning.

2Realistic Expectations

I want you to hold the truth gently but clearly, so you can plan well.

Most channels grow slowly. In the first months, views are often tiny. That is not a verdict on you. It is how a new channel starts, because YouTube has no data yet about who your videos are for.

Many videos get almost no views, and a few get most of them. It is normal for a small number of videos to carry a channel. Your job is to make enough videos to find out which ones.

Income takes time. Even if you reach the eligibility requirements for ads, ad earnings alone are modest for most small channels. Many creators earn more from affiliate links, sponsorships, products and services than from ads.

Full-time is possible, but not typical. Creators who replace a full salary usually have a large audience, several income streams and years of consistent work. Some also have teams. That is the end of a long road, not the start.

Your niche matters. Some topics attract higher advertiser spending, and some audiences are more likely to buy things. But a profitable niche you cannot stand is not a good niche.

Your country matters. Ad rates, payment options and brand budgets differ around the world.

Timelines vary. Here is a rough, honest picture for someone who publishes consistently, about one to two videos a week, with six to ten hours of work. These are ranges, not promises.

StageWhat you are doingTypical time
Choose a niche and set upResearch, channel setup1 to 2 weeks
Learn and publish first videosPlanning, filming, editingMonths one to three
Find what worksReading analytics and improvingMonths three to six
Reach a first small audienceA few hundred to a few thousand subscribers, sometimesOften months six to eighteen, and not guaranteed
Meet monetization requirementsDepends on current rulesOften a year or more
First meaningful incomeCombination of sourcesOften a year or more, and not guaranteed

Some channels grow faster, and many grow slower. Plan for a long game.

What "full-time" really takes

To make a living from YouTube, you generally need most of the following: a clear niche, a library of videos that keep getting watched, a growing audience that trusts you, at least two or three income streams, good records and systems, savings or another income during the slow years and the stamina to keep going for a long time. It is a business, not a lottery ticket.

A channel is not built from one video. It is built from the habit of making the next one a little better.
Reality Check 👀 Please do not quit your job or spend your savings on a channel. Build it alongside your essential income, and make big decisions only when your numbers and savings support them. Read What To Build Before Quitting Your 9 To 5.

Why YouTube is still worth it

For all these cautions, YouTube has real strengths. Videos can be found for years, so your work keeps working. You can build trust quickly, because people see and hear you. It supports many income routes. It rewards helpfulness. And the skills you build, such as speaking, planning, editing and teaching, are valuable in many other places, including jobs, freelancing and your own business.

You do not have to show your face

Many successful channels use only a voice, hands, a screen recording, simple animation, text on screen or product shots. Choose the format that feels sustainable. A face can help build connection, but it is not required.

3Find Your Niche

This is where many channels are won or lost. A clear niche tells YouTube who to show your videos to, tells viewers why to subscribe and tells brands why you matter. Let us find yours properly.

What a niche is, and why it matters

A niche is a specific topic and a specific viewer. "Lifestyle" is a broad topic. "Slow, simple routines for busy students" is a niche. "Food" is broad. "Budget meals for students living in shared kitchens" is a niche.

A clear niche helps in four ways. Viewers know what to expect, so they subscribe. YouTube can understand who might like your videos. Your content ideas become easier to find. And income paths, such as affiliate links and products, become clearer.

A niche is not a prison. You can broaden over time, once you have an audience that trusts you. Start narrow.

The three-circle method

Draw three overlapping circles.

Circle one: what I know or can learn. Skills, experiences and things people ask you about.

Circle two: what I can talk about for a year without getting bored. Topics you will not resent by month four.

Circle three: what people search for, watch and spend money on. Problems and interests with real demand.

Where all three overlap is a promising niche.

Ten questions to sharpen your niche

1. Who exactly am I making videos for? Age, situation, stage of life. 2. What problem or interest brings them to YouTube? 3. What result do they want? To cook faster, study better, organise a small home, learn a skill, save money. 4. Why me? Your experience, style, honesty or angle. 5. What can I make thirty videos about? If you cannot list thirty ideas, narrow or broaden slightly. 6. Can I make this with the tools I have? 7. Do people already watch this? Search for it. 8. Is there room for a different angle? 9. Are there ways to earn in this niche? Affiliate products, services, products, sponsors. 10. Would I be proud to be known for this?

Check demand honestly

  • Search YouTube. Type your topic and related phrases. Notice the suggestions that appear as you type. They show what people actually search for.
  • Look at similar channels. Do small channels get steady views? If so, there is room. If only giants appear, narrow your angle.
  • Read comments. What do viewers ask for, complain about or wish existed?
  • Check other platforms. Are people asking questions about this topic in groups and communities?
  • Watch trends carefully. A topic can look busy because of one viral moment. Look for long-term, steady interest.

A bit of competition is a good sign. It means people care. No competition at all can mean no demand.

Examples of niches, all made up

  • Budget meal prep for students in shared kitchens.
  • Calm study routines for university students.
  • Simple skincare explained for dry skin.
  • Small-space home organising.
  • Beginner spreadsheet tutorials for small businesses.
  • Modest outfit ideas for work.
  • Learning English through everyday conversations.
  • Gentle morning routines for busy mums.
  • Honest reviews of free design tools.
  • Starting a small online business, one week at a time.

Notice how specific they are. Specific is easier to find, easier to plan and easier to earn from.

Niche scoring table

Score each idea from one to five.

QuestionNiche ANiche BNiche C
Do I know who it is for?
Do people search for or watch it?
Can I make thirty video ideas?
Would I enjoy this for a year?
Can I make it with my tools?
Are there ways to earn from it?
Total

Use the scores to think, not to decide for you.

4Know Your Viewer

Once you have a niche, describe the person you are making videos for. This one habit improves everything: titles, hooks, scripts and thumbnails.

Your ideal viewer profile

Give her a name, an age, a situation, a problem and a goal. For example: "Chioma, 22, a university student sharing a kitchen. She has little money and little time. She wants meals that are cheap, filling and not boring." Then ask:

  • What does she search for?
  • What frustrates her?
  • What words does she use to describe her problem?
  • What would make her click?
  • What would make her subscribe?
  • What does she already know, and what does she not?

Imagine you are making each video for Chioma alone.

Listen to real people

Read comments on similar videos. Ask friends who match your viewer what they struggle with. Note the exact words they use. Those words are your titles, your hooks and your descriptions.

Your positioning: what makes you different

Positioning is how you stand out. Ask: What can I offer that is different? It could be your calm style, your honesty, your experience, your focus on a very specific problem or your way of explaining. Write one sentence: "Unlike many channels that [common approach], I [my difference]."

For example: "Unlike many food channels that use expensive ingredients, I only cook with things you can buy at a local market."

Your channel promise

Write one sentence: "This channel helps [who] to [achieve what] through [what kind of videos]."

Example: "This channel helps students cook cheap, filling meals through short, calm, step-by-step videos."

Put this on a sticky note. Every video should serve this promise.

Playbook Note

Private — saved only in this browser.

Your small task. Fill in the niche scoring table for your top three ideas, choose one, and write your channel promise and ideal viewer profile.

5Set Up Your Channel

Your channel is your shop window. When someone lands on it, they decide in seconds whether you look clear and trustworthy.

Create the channel

Sign in to YouTube with a Google account you control and create a channel. Use a strong, unique password and turn on two-step verification, because losing access to a channel is painful. Use an email address you will keep. Check current setup options, because menus change.

Choose your name and handle

Your channel name should be easy to say, spell and remember. It can be your own name or a brand name. If you choose a brand name, make sure it fits where you want to go, not only where you are today. Avoid names that are very long, full of numbers or hard to pronounce. Check that the handle is available and that no similar channel could confuse people. Changing names later is possible but can confuse viewers.

Your profile picture and banner

Use a clear, well-lit photo of your face, or a simple logo or illustration. Make sure it is recognisable when tiny. Your banner is the large image at the top of your channel. Keep it simple: your channel name, your promise and perhaps your upload schedule. Use a free design tool and check the recommended sizes in YouTube's current guidance so that it looks right on phones and televisions.

Your channel description

Your about section should answer: who is this for, what will they find here, how often do you post and how can they contact you? Use keywords naturally, such as "budget meals for students." Add a professional email for business enquiries, links to your other pages and a short, friendly welcome.

A template:

"Hi, I am [name]. This channel helps [who] to [result] through [type of videos]. New videos every [day]. For business enquiries: [email]. Subscribe if you would like [benefit]."

Channel trailer or welcome video

A short video for people who are not yet subscribers. Keep it under about a minute. Say who you are, who the channel is for, what viewers will get and invite them to subscribe. You can add it later, once you have a few videos.

Channel layout and playlists

Organise your videos into playlists by topic, such as "Budget Breakfasts" and "One-Pot Dinners." Playlists help viewers keep watching and help YouTube understand your content. You can feature your best playlist on your channel home page.

Links and contact

Add links to your other accounts and to a page where people can find more of your work. Add a business email. Do not publish personal details such as your home address or phone number.

Safety and privacy

Think about what you show. Avoid revealing your home address, school, workplace or daily routine. Be careful with filming other people, especially children, without permission. Blur or avoid showing documents, screens with private details and street numbers. Learn how to moderate comments, block abusive accounts and hold comments for review. Your wellbeing matters, and you are allowed to protect it.

Channel setup checklist

6Study The Landscape: Learn From Other Channels

Before you make your first video, spend a few hours learning from channels in your niche. You are not copying. You are learning the language of your audience.

Choose ten channels

Find five channels that are larger than yours will be for a while, and five smaller ones, with fewer than a few thousand subscribers. Smaller channels teach you what is possible for a beginner.

What to study

For each channel, note:

  • Their promise. Who is it for?
  • Their top videos. Which got the most views, and why?
  • Their titles and thumbnails. What patterns do you see? What makes you click?
  • Their openings. How do they start the first ten seconds?
  • Their length and structure. How long are the videos, and how are they organised?
  • Their comments. What do viewers love, ask for or criticise?
  • Their gaps. What do viewers keep asking for that the channel has not made?

Find your gaps

Gaps are your opportunities: topics that are poorly explained, outdated, too complicated, too expensive or ignoring a certain type of viewer. If five channels explain "how to meal prep" with expensive ingredients, there may be room for "meal prep on a very small budget."

Build a bank of fifty video ideas

Use these sources:

  • YouTube search suggestions. Type your topic and note the suggestions.
  • Comments. Every question is a video.
  • Your own experience. Problems you solved and mistakes you made.
  • Beginner questions. "What I wish I knew before I started [topic]."
  • Comparisons. "Two ways to do X."
  • Lists. "Five mistakes beginners make with [topic]."
  • Step-by-step tutorials. "How to [specific task] in [time]."
  • Reviews and tests. Honest opinions on tools or methods you have tried.
  • Myths. "People say X, but here is what actually happens."
  • Series. A week-long challenge or a set of connected videos.

Keep your ideas in a spreadsheet with columns: idea, who it is for, the question it answers, search phrase, format and status. Aim for fifty. You will not make them all, but a full list removes the "what do I film?" panic.

Your small task. Study five channels using the list above. Write down three gaps and add ten video ideas to your bank.

7Your Toolkit

You do not need a studio. You need a way to record clearly and a few habits. Check current features, limits and prices on every tool before relying on it.

What actually matters, in order

1. Sound. Viewers forgive a plain picture much sooner than echoey, noisy or muffled audio. 2. Light. Good light makes a phone look far better than it is. 3. Stability. A steady shot looks professional. 4. Clear framing and a tidy background. 5. Editing basics. Cutting out pauses and mistakes.

Cameras and fancy lenses come after all of these.

The free starter kit

What you needFree option to start with
CameraYour phone, with a clean lens
LightA window, or a lamp with a bright, soft bulb
SoundA quiet room and your phone close to you
EditingA free editing app or free desktop editing software
ThumbnailsA free design tool with templates
CaptionsYouTube's automatic captions, which you should check and correct
PlanningA free spreadsheet and notes app
ScriptsA free document tool
StorageFree cloud storage, with backups
SecurityA password manager and two-step verification

Cheap upgrades that make the biggest difference

In this order:

1. A clip-on or small microphone. Often the best first purchase. 2. A small tripod or phone stand. 3. A simple soft light, such as a ring light or a small lamp. 4. A plain backdrop. A tidy wall, a neat shelf or a clean sheet. 5. Headphones, so you can hear your own audio.

Do not buy equipment before you have a publishing habit. Gear does not create consistency.

Setting up a corner for filming

You can film in a corner of a bedroom or living room. Face a window if possible, so that soft daylight falls on your face or your work surface. Avoid sitting with a bright window behind you. Remove clutter from the background. Turn off fans, air conditioners and noisy appliances. Put your phone on a stand at eye level. Do a short test recording and listen with headphones.

Faceless setups

If you do not want to show your face, you can film your hands and a tabletop, record your screen, use a voiceover over footage or still images that you own or have rights to, or create animated or text-based videos. The same rules apply: clear sound and clean visuals.

AI tools

AI assistants can help you brainstorm ideas, outline videos and draft scripts. They can also invent facts and produce generic text. Use them as helpers, then rewrite in your own words, check every fact and follow YouTube's current policies about disclosing altered or synthetic content. See How To Use ChatGPT And Claude To Build Real Income Streams.

Organise your files

Create a folder called "Channel" with subfolders: Ideas, Scripts, Raw Footage, Edits, Thumbnails, Music and Licences, Analytics and Money Records. Name files clearly, for example "2026-03-BudgetPasta-v2." Back up your footage and projects in at least two places. A lost hard drive can erase months of work.

Keep your tools few

Choose one tool for each job and begin. Comparing tools for weeks is a way to avoid making a video. If you want to strengthen the basics, read Digital Skills For Beginners.

8Plan Your Videos

Good videos start before the camera. Planning saves hours, keeps your channel clear and helps you finish what you start.

Choose the video type

Different formats suit different goals.

TypeExampleGood for
Tutorial or how-to"How to make a monthly budget in a spreadsheet"Search traffic and trust
List"Five free tools every beginner needs"Easy structure, wide appeal
Review or comparison"Two free design tools compared"Affiliate links and decisions
Story or experience"What I learned in my first month freelancing"Connection
Challenge or series"Seven days of cheap dinners"Return viewers
Answer a question"Do you need a degree to start freelancing?"Search traffic
Behind the scenes or vlog"A day in my study routine"Personality and community

Beginners often do best with tutorials, lists and answers to real questions, because they match what people search for.

The one-promise rule

Each video should make one clear promise to one clear viewer. "This video will show you how to cook three cheap dinners with rice and eggs." If you cannot say it in one sentence, simplify.

A simple video brief

Before you write a script, fill in this brief.

1. Working title: 2. Who is it for? 3. What question does it answer or what result does it give? 4. What will the viewer know or be able to do at the end? 5. The hook (first ten seconds): 6. The three to five main points: 7. The call to action: 8. Length target: 9. Resources and links to include:

Choose a sensible length

Length should match the promise. A quick answer may take three minutes. A step-by-step tutorial may take ten. Do not stretch a video to hit a number, and do not rush an explanation that needs time. Viewers care about whether the video wastes their time, not the clock.

Structure that holds attention

A reliable structure for many videos:

1. Hook (0 to 15 seconds). Show the result or promise, and why it matters. 2. Quick context (15 to 30 seconds). Who this is for and what you will cover. 3. Main content. Steps, points or demonstrations in a clear order. Signal progress with phrases like "step two." 4. Recap (short). The key takeaway. 5. Call to action. One clear next step, such as watching a related video or subscribing.

Write strong hooks

The first seconds decide whether people stay. Good hooks are honest and specific. Formulas that work in many niches:

  • The promise: "In the next five minutes, I will show you how to cook three dinners for the price of one."
  • The problem: "If you have ever stared into a nearly empty fridge and felt stuck, this is for you."
  • The result first: Show the finished dish, the finished spreadsheet or the finished design, then say "here is how."
  • The mistake: "The biggest mistake beginners make with [topic] is..."
  • The question: "Why does your budget fall apart every month?"
  • The story: "Last month, I almost gave up, and here is what changed."

Avoid long intros, logos or "hi guys, welcome back to my channel" before the point. Greet viewers briefly after you have given them a reason to stay.

Keep promises

Your title and hook make a promise. Deliver it, early and clearly. Misleading titles may bring clicks, but they make people leave, which hurts your channel and trust.

9Script Without Sounding Stiff

A script helps you stay clear and calm. It does not have to be written word for word. It has to help you speak naturally.

Three scripting styles

Full script. Every word written. Useful for beginners who feel nervous, for tutorials and for voiceovers. Read it aloud and edit it to sound like you speaking, not like you writing.

Bullet script. Key points and a few exact lines, such as the hook and the call to action. Good once you are comfortable.

Outline only. Just the structure. Best for experienced speakers or relaxed vlogs.

Most beginners do well with a full script for the hook and the call to action, and bullets for the middle.

Write for the ear

  • Use short sentences.
  • Use simple words.
  • Say "you" and "I."
  • Read it aloud. If you stumble, rewrite.
  • Cut filler.
  • Use examples and little stories.

A script template

Hook: [one or two sentences with the promise]

Context: "I am [name], and in this video I will show you [what]. This is for [who]."

Main point one: [explain, then show an example]

Main point two: [explain, then show an example]

Main point three: [explain, then show an example]

Recap: "So to recap, [three points in one sentence each]."

Call to action: "If this helped, watch [related video] next, and I will see you there."

Add visuals as you write

Next to each line, note what the viewer will see: your face, your hands, a screen recording, text on screen or a diagram. Changing what is on screen every few seconds keeps interest, as long as it serves the content.

Be accurate and honest

Check facts, prices and claims. Be careful with health, money, legal and safety topics, and do not give advice you are not qualified to give. Say when something is your opinion or experience. Correct mistakes in a pinned comment or description if you find them later.

Batch your preparation

Plan and script several videos in one session. For example, spend one evening on ideas, briefs and scripts for four videos. Then film in a second session and edit in a third. Batching keeps you consistent without exhausting you.

A made-up script excerpt

Here is a short, made-up example for a tutorial.

"If your money disappears before the end of the month and you do not know where it went, this simple spreadsheet will show you in ten minutes. I am Ruth, and I will show you how to set it up step by step. By the end, you will have a monthly budget you can use on your phone. Step one: open a new spreadsheet and name three columns: item, category and amount..."

Notice how the hook gives a promise, the context says who it is for and the steps begin quickly.

Your small task. Choose one video from your idea bank. Fill in the video brief, write the hook and the call to action word for word and outline the main points.

10Your First Ten Videos, Planned

The hardest part of a new channel is the blank page. So let us plan your first ten videos using a simple pattern that works for many niches. The pattern is designed to help you learn quickly, serve search, build trust and give viewers a reason to subscribe. Replace the examples with your own niche.

The pattern

VideoPurposeExample, for a budget meals channel
1A simple answer to a very specific question"What To Cook With Only Rice And Eggs"
2A beginner's guide"Budget Cooking For Absolute Beginners"
3A list video"Five Cheap Dinners For One Person"
4A mistakes video"Five Mistakes That Make Student Cooking Expensive"
5A tutorial with a printable or resource"How To Plan A Week Of Meals On A Small Budget"
6A comparison"Cooking In One Pot Versus Two Pans"
7A story or experience"What I Learned From One Month Of Cooking Cheaply"
8A response to a viewer question"You Asked: How Do I Stop Food Going Off?"
9A series starter"Seven Days Of Cheap Dinners, Day One"
10Your best topic, improvedA better version of the video that performed best

You do not have to follow it exactly. It gives you a balance of search-led, trust-building and community-building videos.

Why start with a very specific question

A video titled "Budget Cooking" competes with thousands of others. A video titled "What To Cook With Only Rice And Eggs" competes with far fewer, and it is easier for a new channel to be found. Specific beats general, especially at the start.

Fill in the table for your niche

Copy the table into a spreadsheet and write your own ten titles. For each, add:

  • The viewer's question.
  • The search phrase. Use search suggestions to find it.
  • The hook. One or two sentences.
  • The call to action.
  • The resource or link. A free checklist, a template or a related video.

A made-up first month

Here is a gentle schedule for the first month, assuming one video a week:

  • Week one. Plan and publish video one, the very specific answer.
  • Week two. Plan and publish video two, the beginner's guide. Review early analytics from video one.
  • Week three. Publish video three, the list. Improve the hook based on what you learned.
  • Week four. Publish video four, the mistakes video. Review your first month and plan month two.

If one video a week is too much, publish one every two weeks. A slower schedule you keep is better than a faster one you abandon.

Use each video to learn something

Give each of your first ten videos a small learning goal:

1. Can I make a clear, short video from start to finish? 2. Is my sound clear? 3. Is my hook strong? 4. Does my title match what people search for? 5. Is my thumbnail clear when small? 6. Do people watch past the first thirty seconds? 7. Do people ask follow-up questions? 8. Do viewers subscribe? 9. Can I keep to my schedule? 10. What topic do viewers respond to most?

Write a few lines after each video. These notes teach you more than a course.

Make a simple series

A series is a set of connected videos, such as "Seven Days Of Cheap Dinners" or "Spreadsheet Skills For Small Business, Part One." Series encourage viewers to keep watching and subscribe for the next one. They also give you a plan, because you already know the next idea.

Repurpose what you make

Every video can become several things:

  • A few short clips for Shorts and other platforms.
  • A blog post or checklist.
  • A free resource for your email list.
  • A pinned comment or a community post.
  • A script for a follow-up video that answers viewers' questions.

Repurposing multiplies the value of each video without multiplying your work.

11Shorts, Community And Consistency

Three things help a young channel grow gently: short videos, a real relationship with viewers and a rhythm you can keep.

Shorts as tasters

Shorts are short, vertical videos that appear in a swipeable feed. They can introduce your channel to new people who might later watch your long videos.

How to use them well:

  • One idea per Short. A single tip, trick or moment.
  • A strong first second. Start with the interesting part, not an introduction.
  • Text on screen, because many people watch without sound.
  • Vertical framing and clear visuals.
  • A call to action. Invite people to watch the full video, if it fits, or to follow for more tips.
  • Honesty. Do not mislead people with clips that do not match what the long video contains.

You can cut Shorts from your long videos, or film them separately. Check current rules, features and monetisation details for Shorts, as they differ from long-form videos and change often.

Build a real relationship with viewers

  • Reply to comments, especially in the first hours after you publish. Ask questions back.
  • Use viewer questions as video ideas, and credit the question when you answer it, if the viewer is comfortable.
  • Pin a helpful comment with links and a question.
  • Use community posts, if available, to ask what your viewers want next.
  • Be consistent in tone. Viewers return for the way you make them feel as much as for the topic.
  • Set boundaries. You do not need to answer every message or accept every request. Decide what you will and will not engage with.

Real relationships matter more than raw numbers. A small, engaged community is the foundation for everything else, including income.

Consistency without burnout

Consistency does not mean working every day. It means keeping a rhythm you can sustain. Here is a simple weekly rhythm for about eight hours a week:

DayTaskTime
MondayPlan: choose the video, fill in the brief45 minutes
TuesdayScript and prepare90 minutes
WednesdayFilm90 minutes
ThursdayEdit120 minutes
FridayTitle, thumbnail, description and publish60 minutes
WeekendReply to comments, share, review analytics45 minutes

Adjust it to your life. If you only have four hours, make a video every two weeks.

Build a buffer

A buffer is a stock of finished videos. Once you can, aim to be a video or two ahead of schedule. A buffer protects you when life gets busy, when you are ill or when you simply need a rest.

Plan your breaks

Decide in advance when you will take breaks, such as a week off every couple of months. Tell your viewers if you are going to be away. A planned rest is part of a sustainable channel.

Celebrate small wins

A first comment from a stranger, a viewer saying "this helped," a video getting found through search: these are real signs of progress. Write them in a notebook. On hard days, read them.

Your small task. Fill in your first-ten-videos table with your own niche. Choose your publishing rhythm, and write the first four weeks of your schedule.

12Film Your Videos

Now let us film. The aim is clear, simple footage, not perfection. Your tenth video will be better than your first, and you only get to the tenth by making the first.

Before you press record: a short checklist

Filming tips that make the biggest difference

Start with a clap or a clear pause. It makes cutting easier.

Record in short chunks. Film each section separately. If you make a mistake, repeat only that section.

Speak slightly slower and clearer than normal. Smile when it suits you. Warmth carries through a camera.

Look at the lens when you speak, and at your work when you demonstrate.

Frame yourself with a little space above your head, and keep important items in the middle of the frame.

Show, do not only tell. Hold products up. Show your screen. Demonstrate the steps.

Capture extra footage. Film a few seconds of close-ups, hands, products or the room. These cutaways help you hide edits and keep interest.

Record clean audio. If you can, record a few seconds of the room's silence. It helps with noise reduction later.

Film your hook last or twice. You will know best what the video promised after you have made it.

Filming with a voiceover

If you prefer not to speak on camera, film your actions or screen and record the voiceover afterwards in a quiet space. Read your script slowly, and record in short sections.

Filming safely and respectfully

  • Do not film in places where filming is not allowed, and ask permission in private spaces.
  • Ask before filming other people, especially children, and check local rules.
  • Avoid showing street signs, ID cards, bills, passwords and private screens.
  • Be careful about revealing your location or routines.

Filming rhythm

Many creators film all their videos for a week in one session. Dress in similar clothes if you want to film several videos in the same look, or change tops for variety. Keep a "filming day" list of videos, props and outfits. Rest between takes and drink water. A tired voice is a thin voice.

13Edit Your Videos

Editing is where a rough recording becomes something watchable. The good news is that simple editing is enough to start.

The basic editing steps

1. Import your footage into a free editing tool and organise it. 2. Rough cut. Remove mistakes, long pauses and repeated takes. Keep the best take of each section. 3. Tighten the pace. Cut filler words and dead air. A video that moves feels more professional. 4. Add visuals. Cutaways, screen recordings, text overlays and simple graphics where they help. 5. Add on-screen text for key points, steps and names. 6. Fix the sound. Balance voice and music, remove obvious noise and keep volume consistent. 7. Add music, if any, at a low level that does not compete with your voice. Use only music you have the right to use. 8. Add captions. Review them for accuracy. 9. Add an end screen. A short ending with a suggestion for the next video. 10. Export at the recommended settings, and watch the whole video before uploading.

The edit that matters most: the first thirty seconds

Spend extra time on your hook and the first thirty seconds. Cut every unnecessary word. Show the payoff early. Make sure the title, thumbnail and opening all match. If viewers leave in the first moments, your video is unlikely to be shown to many more people.

Pace and variety

Change the shot, the angle, the text or the visual every few seconds, as long as it fits the content. Too many effects distract, and too few cause boredom. Watch videos in your niche and notice how often they change what is on screen.

Music, sounds and copyright

Copyright protects music, clips, images and more. Do not use popular songs or clips from films, TV shows or other creators without permission. Use music from libraries that you are allowed to use on YouTube, and read their licence terms. YouTube offers its own audio library for creators, and many free and paid music services exist. Keep a record of where each track came from and what the licence says. A copyright claim can block, mute or monetise your video for someone else, and repeated problems can affect your channel.

Stock footage and images

The same rules apply. Check the licence for every clip, image and font, and keep records. When in doubt, film or create your own.

Captions and accessibility

Captions help people who are deaf or hard of hearing, people watching without sound and viewers who are not fluent in your language. YouTube can generate automatic captions, but they often contain mistakes, so check and correct them. Use clear speech, readable text and good contrast.

A simple editing workflow

Many creators batch their editing: rough cuts for all videos on one day, then polishing and captions on another. Save project files and exports in clearly named folders. Keep a "template project" with your intro, end screen layout and text styles, so each new video starts with a head start.

14Titles, Thumbnails And Hooks

These three elements decide whether anyone watches your video. A great video with a weak title and thumbnail may never be seen. Let us make them work, honestly.

How they work together

Think of your title, thumbnail and hook as one promise told in three ways. The title and thumbnail make people curious enough to click. The hook confirms that they are in the right place. If any of the three mismatch, people click away, which hurts your video.

Writing titles

A good title is clear, specific and honest, and it usually includes the words people search for.

Formulas that work in many niches:

  • The result: "How To Make A Monthly Budget In A Spreadsheet"
  • The number: "5 Cheap Dinners You Can Make With Rice"
  • The question: "Do You Need A Degree To Start Freelancing?"
  • The beginner angle: "Skincare For Dry Skin: A Beginner's Guide"
  • The specific outcome: "How I Organised My Tiny Kitchen For Almost Nothing"
  • The comparison: "Two Free Design Tools Compared"

Tips.

  • Put the most important words early.
  • Keep it short enough to read on a phone.
  • Use plain words.
  • Include the main search phrase naturally.
  • Be honest. Avoid exaggerations like "SHOCKING" if they are not true.
  • Test two or three versions and choose the clearest.

Look at your search suggestions and at what similar videos use. Your title should be at least as clear, and ideally clearer.

Designing thumbnails

A thumbnail is a tiny poster. People see it at a small size on a phone, so simple wins.

Principles.

  • One idea. One clear subject.
  • High contrast. Text and subject stand out from the background.
  • Large, readable text. Three to five words, at most.
  • A clear face or object. If you show your face, make the expression match the video honestly.
  • Consistent style. A few colours and fonts that become recognisable.
  • Honesty. The thumbnail must reflect what the video delivers.
  • Check it small. Shrink it to the size of a postage stamp and see if it still works.

Use a free design tool with templates. Make a thumbnail template that you can reuse. Do not use images you have no right to use, and avoid misleading or inappropriate imagery.

Descriptions

Write a clear description. The first lines appear most prominently, so put the main promise and a short summary there. Include relevant keywords naturally, links to resources, chapters if you use them, any disclosures and a short call to action. Avoid keyword stuffing or unrelated tags. Check current best practice and policies.

Chapters, captions, cards and end screens

  • Chapters divide your video into labelled sections, helping viewers jump around.
  • Captions are the on-screen text of your speech.
  • Cards are small prompts that can link to other videos.
  • End screens appear at the end and suggest another video or ask for a subscription.

Check current features and rules before using them.

Playlists

Group related videos into playlists. Put your best, most helpful videos first. Playlists help people keep watching and help you shape the experience on your channel.

Shorts

Shorts are short vertical videos that appear in a swipeable feed. They can introduce new people to your channel. Keep them quick, with a strong first second, a single idea and simple text. Many creators use Shorts as taster videos that lead to longer videos on the same topic. Check current rules and monetisation details for Shorts, because they differ from long-form videos.

Publish with care

Before you press publish:

You can also schedule videos, which helps you keep a regular rhythm.

After publishing

Reply to early comments, share the video with your warm network and relevant communities where allowed and keep an eye on analytics over the first days and weeks. Do not delete and re-upload videos in a panic. Give each one time.

15Read Your Analytics

Analytics can feel overwhelming. Focus on a few measures that tell you what to do next.

The key numbers

Impressions and click-through rate. How often your thumbnail was shown, and how often it was clicked. A low click-through rate suggests the title or thumbnail needs work. Rates vary widely by niche and by where the video is shown, so compare your own videos with each other rather than with a fixed number.

Average view duration and audience retention. How long people watch, and where they drop off. If many leave in the first thirty seconds, strengthen your hook. If they drop at one particular point, ask what happened there.

Traffic sources. Where viewers came from: search, browse, suggested videos or external links. This tells you where your videos are being found.

Search terms. The words people typed before finding your video, if shown.

Audience. Who watches: age ranges, locations and when they are online. Check whether this matches your ideal viewer.

Subscribers gained. Which videos bring subscribers?

Returning viewers. Are people coming back?

A simple weekly review

Once a week, spend twenty minutes:

1. Look at the last two or three videos. What was the click-through rate and average view duration? 2. Note the traffic sources and search terms. 3. Read the comments for questions and requests. 4. Write three lines: what to do more of, what to do less of and what to try next.

Use data to guide, not to rule

Early numbers are small and noisy. Do not conclude too much from a handful of views. Look for patterns across several videos over weeks. And remember that numbers measure behaviour, not your worth.

What to do when a video does well

Study why. Was it the topic, the title, the thumbnail or the hook? Make a follow-up that answers the next question viewers will have. Add a playlist. Link it from related videos. Share it in your email or other platforms.

What to do when a video does poorly

Ask: Was it shown to people (impressions)? If few, the topic may not match search demand. Was it clicked (click-through rate)? If not, improve the title and thumbnail. Was it watched (retention)? If not, tighten the hook and the structure. Sometimes a title and thumbnail change can help an older video. Learn from it and move on.

Your small task. Film and edit one short video using the checklists in this chapter, write three title options, design one thumbnail and look at its analytics after a week.

16Get Monetized: Every Real Way A Channel Earns

This is the chapter that decides whether your channel becomes a hobby, a side income or something bigger. Almost every successful creator earns from several sources, not just one. Let us walk through them honestly, from the ones available soonest to those that take time.

Income route one: your own services

This is often the fastest route, because it does not depend on your view count. Your channel becomes a shop window for a skill. If you teach budgeting, you might offer budgeting sessions. If you show design, you might offer design services to small businesses. If you share organising tips, you might offer home organising consultations.

How it works: viewers see your expertise, trust you and ask how to hire you. Add a clear line in your description and channel about services, and a simple contact method. See How To Get Your First Freelance Client.

Be careful in sensitive areas such as health, mental health, legal and financial advice. Do not offer services you are not qualified to provide, and follow the rules in your country.

Income route two: affiliate links

An affiliate link is a special link that tracks purchases made through it, and you earn a commission. You can add them to descriptions and mention products in videos.

How it works: you recommend products you genuinely use, with honest pros and cons, and include your link. When someone buys, you earn a small commission.

Rules and good practice:

  • Disclose clearly. Say in the video and in the description that you may earn a commission. Many countries and YouTube's own policies require it.
  • Only recommend what you use or have good reason to trust.
  • Read each programme's terms, including payout rules, country eligibility and any restrictions on where you can place links.
  • Do not promise results. Avoid exaggerated claims.
  • Keep your links updated, since products change.

Affiliate income grows with trust and search traffic, so tutorials, reviews and comparisons work well.

Income route three: your own digital products

Once you know what your viewers struggle with, you can create products: templates, planners, guides, checklists or mini-courses. Videos explain the problem and show the product in use, and your description links to it. A product earns every time someone buys, not only when someone watches. Read How To Start And Grow A Profitable Digital Product Business and The Soft Girl's Guide To Passive Income.

Income route four: ads through the YouTube Partner Programme

The YouTube Partner Programme lets eligible channels earn a share of ad revenue and use certain features. To join, channels must meet eligibility requirements, which have included a minimum number of subscribers and watch hours or Shorts views, and must follow YouTube's policies. The thresholds and tiers have changed over time and differ in some countries, so check YouTube's current requirements on its official help pages.

Points to know:

  • Ad earnings per view vary hugely by niche, country, season and audience. Do not rely on a single "average" figure.
  • Your content must follow advertiser-friendly guidelines to earn full ad revenue.
  • Payment depends on your country, tax information and a payment threshold.
  • For most small channels, ad income is modest. It is a useful bonus, not usually the main income, especially early.

Income route five: channel memberships, fan funding and other platform tools

YouTube has offered features that let viewers support creators directly, such as paid memberships or tipping tools. Eligibility, features and availability change and differ by country. Check current options. If you offer memberships, remember that you are promising ongoing value, so decide what members get and make sure you can deliver it without burning out.

Income route six: brand sponsorships and partnerships

A sponsorship is a paid arrangement in which a brand pays you to feature or mention its product. This usually comes after you have a clear niche and an audience that matches the brand's customers. Small channels can win deals, especially with small and local brands, if their audience is engaged and specific.

How to prepare:

  • A clear niche and honest audience data. Use your analytics.
  • Consistent, good-quality videos.
  • A simple media kit. A one- or two-page document with who you are, your audience, your content, your rates and your contact.
  • A rate card. What you charge for a dedicated video, a mention or a short.
  • Written agreements. Deliverables, dates, fee, payment terms, usage rights, approval process and disclosure.

Disclose sponsorships clearly, using YouTube's paid promotion disclosure tools and wording that follows your country's advertising rules. Only work with brands you believe in, and never overstate what a product can do.

For pricing, think about your time, the deliverables, your audience's value, usage rights and exclusivity. Rates vary enormously, so research your market, and do not rely on a single formula. The free Freelance Rate Calculator can help you think about your time.

Income route seven: UGC and production work

If you become good at filming and editing, you can offer those skills to brands or other creators, such as editing videos, making thumbnails or filming product content. Your channel works as a portfolio.

Income route eight: licensing your content

If you create original footage or videos that others might want to use, you may be able to license them. This is advanced and uncommon for beginners. Make sure you own all rights, and check agreements carefully.

Putting it together: a made-up income stack

Take Funmi, a made-up example, who runs a channel about simple budgeting. In her first year, her income comes from a few paid budgeting sessions to viewers, a template she sells and a few affiliate commissions from tools she genuinely uses. In her second year, she meets the requirements for ads and earns a little from them. In her third, a small brand pays her for a sponsored video. No single source is large. Together, they make a growing side income, and she understands each one.

A realistic order of operations

StageIncome routes to focus on
Months one to sixServices and your own small products, honest affiliate links, no expectations of ad income
Months six to eighteenAdd affiliate content, a product, and ads or memberships when eligible
Year two onwardAdd sponsorships, collaborations and a broader product line

Everything depends on your channel. Some creators move faster, and many move slower.

Keep records and think about taxes

Record every payment, expense and deal. Many countries expect you to report income from online sources, and YouTube may ask for tax information. Rules differ and change, so check official guidance for your country, and consider speaking to a qualified person. Keep a separate pot for tax money. Read Budget Like A Queen for a beginner's money system.

Rules, copyright and community guidelines

Follow YouTube's community guidelines and monetization policies. Do not use music or clips you do not have the right to use. Be honest in your titles and thumbnails. Do not buy views or subscribers, since this breaks the rules and does not help you. Avoid reused content with no value added. Be careful about content that mentions children. YouTube's policies change, so check them regularly, and keep a note of key rules.

Build your money idea

Fill in these lines.

1. My channel promise: 2. My first income route (services, affiliate or product): 3. What I will offer, in one sentence: 4. How viewers will find the offer (description, pinned comment, end screen): 5. My honest affiliate products, if any: 6. My plan to check monetization requirements: 7. My record-keeping system: 8. My review date:

Your small task. Choose your first income route, write the one-sentence offer and add a short line about it to your channel description.

17Where To Go: Getting Your Videos Seen

YouTube is not the only place your videos can be found. Sharing them thoughtfully in other places helps you get early views and signals, and builds a community around your channel. You do not need all of these. Choose your warm network and two or three others.

Your warm network (start here)

Your warm network is everyone who already knows you: friends, family, classmates, colleagues and community groups. Ask a few people to watch a video and tell you what was clear and what was confusing. Honest feedback is worth more than a hundred polite likes. Do not pressure anyone to subscribe, and never ask for fake engagement.

A message: "Hi Zainab, I have made a short video about cooking cheap dinners for students. Would you watch it and tell me what you think? Here is the link: [link]. Honest feedback would really help."

Instagram

Share short clips, behind-the-scenes content and teasers that lead to your full video. Reels, stories and posts can reach people who do not know you yet. Read Instagram Pays Too, Sis.

TikTok

Short clips can introduce new people to your style and topics. Make clear, standalone short videos that tease your longer content. Check platform rules about links and promotion.

Pinterest

Pinterest is a visual search engine. Pins that link to your videos, with clear titles and good images, can bring steady visitors over time, especially for tutorials, recipes, planners and ideas.

LinkedIn

LinkedIn suits professional and business topics. Share short lessons and link to relevant videos. See Babe, Your Next International Opportunity Is On LinkedIn.

X (formerly Twitter)

Useful for sharing short tips, updates and replies, and for connecting with other creators.

Facebook groups

Groups exist for almost every interest. Read the rules, help others and share your videos only where promotion is allowed.

Reddit

Communities exist for many topics, but many ban self-promotion. Contribute honestly, answer questions and share a video only when it truly helps and the rules allow it.

Your email list

An email list is the most valuable place you can build. Offer a small free gift, such as a checklist related to a video, in exchange for an email address, and email people when you publish. Check your country's rules about consent and unsubscribing.

Collaborations

Collaborate with creators of a similar size in a related niche: guest appearances, shared videos, shout-outs or answering each other's questions. Choose partners whose values and audience match yours, and agree on the details in writing.

Blogs and websites

A simple blog or website that embeds your videos and answers related questions can bring search traffic and give you a place to collect emails and sell products.

Local and in-person

If your niche suits it, local groups, schools, shops and events can be a source of early viewers.

How to choose

Ask: Where do my viewers already spend time? Where can I show up weekly without dreading it? Choose your warm network, one short-video platform and your email list.

18Scripts You Can Copy

A script removes the blank-screen panic. Every example is made up. Change the details until it sounds like you.

The kind and legal way to reach out

Be respectful. Send personal messages, not copy-paste blasts. Say who you are and why you are writing. Make it easy to say no, and stop if someone asks you to. Rules about unsolicited messages and emails differ by country and platform, so check them. Do not ask for or trade subscribers or views, because it breaks platform rules and does not help you.

A message to your warm network.

"Hi [Name], I have started a YouTube channel about [topic]. My latest video is about [what]. If you have a few minutes, I would really appreciate your honest feedback on the first thirty seconds. Here is the link: [link]. Thank you!"

A post announcing a new video.

"New video: [title]. If you have ever struggled with [problem], I show you how to [result] in [time]. Link in my bio. Tell me in the comments what you would like me to cover next."

A pinned comment.

"Thanks for watching! Here are the resources mentioned in this video: [links]. If you have a question, leave it below and I will answer. What should I make next?"

A reply to a viewer's question.

"Great question! In short, [answer]. I will make a full video about this soon, so subscribe if you would like to see it."

An email to a small brand about a sponsorship.

Subject: Collaboration idea for [Brand Name]

"Hello [Name], I am Ruth, and I run a YouTube channel about budget meals for students. I have used your [product] for a few weeks and genuinely like it, and my viewers often ask for affordable kitchen tools. I would love to talk about a paid collaboration, with honest feedback and clear disclosure. My media kit is attached with my audience details and rates. Would you be open to a conversation? Thank you for your time."

A reply when a brand is interested.

"Thank you so much for getting back to me! I would love to work together. To make sure I do this properly, could you tell me what you would like, by when and how the video will be used? I will send a short summary and my rates so we are both clear."

A message to another creator about collaborating.

"Hi [Name], I love your videos on [topic]. I think our audiences overlap nicely. Would you be interested in a simple collaboration, such as answering each other's top viewer questions in a short video? No pressure at all."

A viewer asks about your service.

"Thank you for asking! I offer [service] for [who]. It includes [what] and costs [price]. If you would like details, email me at [email] and I will send a short summary."

Declining a deal that is not right.

"Thank you for thinking of me. After reading the details, I do not think this is the right fit for my audience, so I will pass. I appreciate the opportunity and would love to hear about future collaborations."

Track your outreach

Open a spreadsheet with columns: date, name, platform, what I shared, reply, next step and follow-up date. Updating it weekly turns a stressful task into a calm routine.

19A Sample Media Kit And Sponsorship Checklist

When a brand shows interest, a clear, honest media kit makes you look professional. And a checklist protects you from deals that are not what they seem. Here are both, written out.

A sample media kit, in text form

This is made up. Replace every detail with your own honest information, and keep it to one or two pages.

Chiamaka Eze | Budget Meals For Students YouTube: [your channel link] | Email: [your email]

About the channel. I make calm, step-by-step videos that help students cook cheap, filling meals in shared kitchens. My style is simple, practical and honest. I only recommend products I have used.

My audience. [Number] subscribers. Most viewers are aged [range] and based in [countries], according to my analytics. My most popular videos are tutorials about rice and egg recipes, and my average view duration is [number] minutes. Many viewers ask for kitchen tool recommendations.

What I offer.

  • A dedicated video featuring your product in a real recipe.
  • A short integration inside a related video.
  • A Short or social clip.
  • Usage rights options, with prices on request.

Past work and results. [List a couple of examples, or practice videos labelled honestly, with what they achieved, such as views and comments.]

How I work. I read the brief carefully, send a draft for approval when agreed, disclose all partnerships clearly and deliver on time.

What I will not promote. Products that make unsafe or exaggerated claims, or that I would not use myself.

Contact. Email me to discuss a collaboration, and I will send my rates.

A simple rate card structure

List what you offer, what is included and the price, or "on request." For each item, think about:

  • Time. Planning, filming, editing, revisions and publishing.
  • Deliverables. One video, a mention, a short or a set.
  • Usage rights. Can the brand reuse your video in adverts or on their own channels, and for how long?
  • Exclusivity. Are you barred from working with competitors for a period?
  • Revisions. How many rounds are included?
  • Timeline. Rush jobs cost more.

Rates vary enormously by niche, country and audience, so research what similar creators charge, and start with a fair, modest figure that you can raise.

The sponsorship checklist

Before you say yes to any brand deal, check:

Handling the conversation

When a brand sends an offer, you do not have to answer immediately. You can say, "Thank you, I am interested. Let me review the details and get back to you." If the offer is too low, propose adjustments: a higher fee, fewer deliverables or a shorter usage period. If the budget is fixed and too small, it is fine to decline politely.

A reply you can adapt:

"Thank you for the offer. I would love to work together. For a dedicated video with one round of changes and usage on your organic channels for three months, my fee is [amount]. If you would like to use it in paid adverts or for longer, I can send a quote for extended rights. I will also include a clear paid promotion disclosure. Does that work for you?"

After the video is published

Share results honestly: views, comments and any feedback. Send a thank-you note. Send your invoice with the deliverables, the amount, the date and payment instructions. Follow up politely if payment is late. Keep records of everything. Repeat work with the same brand is often where the real income lies.

20Common Mistakes (And How To Dodge Them)

Everyone makes some of these. Seeing them in advance saves months.

Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake one is starting without a niche. If a viewer cannot tell what your channel is about, they cannot subscribe.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake two is buying expensive gear first. Sound, light and a clear idea matter more.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake three is making videos nobody searches for. Start with questions real people ask.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake four is a weak first thirty seconds. Give the payoff early.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake five is misleading titles and thumbnails. They may bring clicks, but they cost trust and retention.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake six is ignoring sound. Echo and noise make people leave.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake seven is quitting too soon. Most channels need many videos before the first small signals appear.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake eight is posting irregularly with no plan. Choose a rhythm you can keep.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake nine is copying other creators too closely. Learn from them, then add your own angle.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake ten is breaking copyright. Check every song, clip, image and font.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake eleven is chasing views and forgetting income paths. Build services, products or affiliate routes early.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake twelve is buying subscribers, views or "growth services." They break the rules and do not help.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake thirteen is ignoring analytics. Learn from the data, calmly.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake fourteen is burning out. A sustainable pace beats a heroic sprint.

21When Things Do Not Go To Plan: A Troubleshooting Table

What is happeningWhat it usually meansWhat to try
Nobody watches my videosNew channel, unclear topic or weak titlesMake videos that answer real search questions, improve titles and thumbnails and share with your warm network
People click but leave quicklyHook does not match the title or thumbnailRewrite the first thirty seconds and make sure the promise is delivered early
Few people clickWeak title or thumbnailTest clearer titles, simpler thumbnails and better matches to search phrases
I get views but no subscribersNo clear reason to subscribeMake your channel promise clear, add a call to action and make series
My audio is poorEcho, noise or distanceRecord closer to the microphone, use a quiet room and add soft furnishings
I hate being on cameraNormal nervesStart with a voiceover, hands or screen recording, and practise gradually
I cannot keep up with uploadsToo ambitiousReduce frequency, batch tasks and plan a smaller schedule
A video got a copyright claimMusic or clip rights issueRead the notice, replace or remove the content and check your licences
My views suddenly droppedAlgorithm, seasonality or topic changeReview analytics, return to what worked and avoid panic
Negative comments upset meCommon onlineUse moderation tools, block abusers and reply only when helpful
I am not earning yetNormal early onFocus on services, products and affiliate routes while you build toward eligibility
I feel like quittingBurnout or discouragementRest, review your progress, shrink your schedule and talk to a supportive friend
I got a suspicious sponsorship offerPossible scamPause, verify the brand independently and never pay to collaborate
My account was hackedWeak securityFollow YouTube's recovery steps, change passwords, turn on two-step verification and check connected apps

22Scam And Safety Warnings

Once you have a channel, some people will try to take advantage. Learn the patterns early.

Common scams aimed at creators

  • Fake sponsorship and brand deals. A "brand" offers a high fee but asks you to pay for a product, a "registration fee" or "insurance" first.
  • Fake cheque and overpayment scams. You receive a payment larger than agreed and are asked to refund the difference. The original payment later proves fake.
  • Fake copyright and policy-violation messages. Emails claiming your channel will be deleted unless you click a link, log in or share a code.
  • Phishing links in comments or emails. Fake login pages to steal your account.
  • Malicious "collaboration" files. Attachments or links that install harmful software on your computer. Be careful with unexpected files, even from "brands."
  • Fake "verification" or "monetization" services. Someone offers to get you monetised or verified for a fee.
  • Subscriber and view sellers. They take your money, break the rules and may steal your account details.
  • Pay-to-promote schemes. "Channels" that promise to promote your video for a fee.
  • Impersonation. Accounts copying your name and picture to message your viewers.
  • Account takeover attempts. Messages that pretend to be from other creators or YouTube.
  • Get-rich-quick channel courses. Programmes promising six-figure channels if you pay now.

Warning signs

Urgency and pressure. Requests for passwords, codes or payment. Offers that seem far too generous for your size. Strange email addresses and poor spelling. Unexpected attachments. Pressure to move off the platform or to keep the deal secret. Any promise of guaranteed views, subscribers or money.

Safety habits

Use strong, unique passwords and two-step verification for your Google account and your email. Never share login codes. Verify messages by logging in to YouTube yourself, not by clicking links. Open attachments from unknown senders only when you have verified the sender, and keep your devices updated. Do not pay to be paid. Keep agreements in writing. Check payments in your own account, not through screenshots. Back up your videos and projects.

If you think you have been scammed or hacked

Please do not blame yourself. Stop contact. Change your passwords immediately, starting with your email, and turn on two-step verification. Use YouTube's official recovery and security tools. Contact your bank or payment provider if you lost money. Save screenshots and details. Report it to the platform and to the appropriate authority in your country. Tell someone you trust.

Protect your wellbeing

Visible creators sometimes face rude, hurtful or inappropriate comments and messages. Use moderation tools, block and report abusers, and decide in advance what you will and will not engage with. You are allowed to take breaks. If online harassment affects your mental health, talk to someone you trust, and consider professional support. Your wellbeing matters more than any channel.

23Worked Examples

Let us walk through three made-up examples to show how this works in real life. They are teaching examples, not real results.

Example one: Chiamaka, a budget meals channel

Setup. Chiamaka picks a narrow niche: budget meals for students in shared kitchens. Her channel promise: "This channel helps students cook cheap, filling meals through short, calm, step-by-step videos." She uses her phone, a window and a cheap clip-on microphone.

Months one to three. She publishes one video a week, based on questions from student groups. Most get very few views. She improves her hooks and titles each time. One video, "What To Cook With Only Rice And Eggs," starts getting a few views a day from search.

Months four to nine. She makes a short series around rice and eggs. She learns from her analytics that people drop off during long intros, so she cuts them. She offers a free one-week meal planner in her description for emails.

Months ten to eighteen. She sells a small meal-planning template, adds honest affiliate links for kitchen tools she uses and eventually meets the requirements for ads. Her income is modest and spread across several sources.

Lessons. A narrow niche, search-led videos, steady improvement and several small income routes.

Example two: Bisi, a faceless tutorial channel

Setup. Bisi does not want to show her face. She chooses beginner spreadsheet tutorials for small business owners. She records her screen and her voice.

Months one to three. She publishes tutorials such as "How To Make An Invoice In A Spreadsheet." She learns to speak slowly and zoom in on the screen.

Months four to nine. Her videos are found through search. She adds a free invoice template to her descriptions, which grows her email list. A few viewers ask whether she can set up spreadsheets for them.

Months ten to eighteen. She offers a small paid setup service and sells a bundle of templates. Her channel works as her portfolio, and most of her income comes from services and products, not from ads.

Lessons. You do not need to show your face. A helpful, searchable channel can bring clients.

Example three: Ngozi, who avoided a scam

The offer. Ngozi receives an email from a "brand" offering a large payment for a video, but it asks her to pay a "registration fee" and to send her channel login so they can "set up the campaign."

The check. She applies the safety checks. She pauses, searches the brand's name with the word "scam" and notices that the email address does not match the brand's real website. She also notices that no genuine brand would ask for her login.

What she does. She does not reply, reports and deletes the email and tells a friend. She also checks that her own account has two-step verification turned on.

Lessons. No legitimate brand asks for your login or a fee to pay you. Pausing and verifying protects your channel.

Create your own example

Write your own story in five lines: The niche I will choose. My channel promise. My first ten video ideas. My first income route. The date I will review.

24Mindset: The Voices That Show Up

When you start putting yourself on the internet, familiar voices appear. Here is how I answer them.

"Nobody will watch." At first, very few people will, and that is normal. You are not making videos for a crowd. You are making them for the one person who needs them.

"I look and sound strange." Everyone does at first. Almost everyone dislikes hearing their own voice. Keep going, and your comfort will grow.

"Everyone else is better." Many creators began with poor audio and awkward openings. You are seeing their later work, not their first videos.

"I am too old, too young, too shy or too late." There are viewers for all kinds of creators, and there is a place for your voice.

"What if people criticise me?" Some may. Use moderation tools, learn from useful feedback and ignore cruelty.

"I feel like I should be further along." Compare yourself with your own first video, not with a stranger's tenth year.

"It is taking too long." Most channels take a long time. Build a rhythm you can keep, and celebrate small wins.

You do not have to be good at the start. You have to start in order to get good.

25Your First Seven Days: A Gentle Quick Start

About thirty to sixty minutes a day.

Day 1. List ten topics you know or could learn, and ten questions people ask you. Use the three-circle method.

Day 2. Choose your niche and write your channel promise and ideal viewer profile.

Day 3. Create your channel, secure your account with two-step verification and write your about section.

Day 4. Study five channels in your niche and note three gaps. Add ten ideas to your video bank.

Day 5. Set up your filming corner and record a thirty-second test video. Listen back with headphones.

Day 6. Choose your first video, fill in the brief and write the hook and the call to action.

Day 7. Script the main points, and plan when you will film.

26Your Thirty-Day Plan

Here is a full month. About thirty to sixty minutes a day. If you miss a day, simply continue.

Week one: foundation

  • Days 1 to 7: follow the quick start above.

Week two: your first video

  • Day 8: Film your first video in short sections.
  • Day 9: Edit the rough cut.
  • Day 10: Add visuals, captions and music you have the right to use.
  • Day 11: Write three title options and design a thumbnail.
  • Day 12: Watch the whole video, fix problems and write the description.
  • Day 13: Publish, and share with your warm network for honest feedback.
  • Day 14: Review comments and early analytics, and write what you learned.

Week three: your second and third videos

  • Day 15: Plan video two using your brief.
  • Day 16: Script and film video two.
  • Day 17: Edit video two.
  • Day 18: Thumbnail, title and publish video two.
  • Day 19: Plan and script video three.
  • Day 20: Film video three.
  • Day 21: Edit, add a thumbnail and publish video three.

Week four: review and prepare to earn

  • Day 22: Review analytics for all three videos: click-through rate, average view duration, traffic sources.
  • Day 23: Improve the hook of your weakest video, or update a thumbnail.
  • Day 24: Choose your first income route and write the one-sentence offer.
  • Day 25: Add a line about your offer to your description and channel.
  • Day 26: Create a simple free gift or resource for your viewers.
  • Day 27: Start an email sign-up, if you want one, following your country's rules.
  • Day 28: Plan your next four videos.
  • Day 29: Check YouTube's current monetization requirements and note them.
  • Day 30: Review the month and write your next thirty-day goal.

27Your Ninety-Day Plan

Days 1 to 30: set up and publish

Complete the thirty-day plan. By day thirty you should have a clear niche, a set-up channel, three published videos and a plan for your first income route.
