Days 31 to 60: build a rhythm and learn

Publish one video a week. Improve hooks, titles and thumbnails using analytics. Answer comments. Share with your warm network and one or two platforms. Offer your first service or product, honestly, in your description.

Days 61 to 90: grow and refine

Make a follow-up to your best video. Create a playlist for your best topic. Add honest affiliate links to relevant videos, with disclosure. Reach out to one or two small collaborators. Review your numbers, your energy and your income paths, and decide what to do more of next.

Monthly check-in questions

  • How many videos did I publish?
  • Which video did best, and why?
  • What did my analytics tell me about hooks, titles and retention?
  • What did viewers ask for?
  • How much did I earn, spend and keep?
  • What did I enjoy, and what drained me?
  • What will I do more of, less of or differently next month?

28Questions Girls Ask Me

Can I really make a living on YouTube?

Some people do, but it is not typical or fast, and I cannot promise it will happen for you. Most creators who earn a full income combine several sources, such as services, products, affiliate links, sponsorships and ads, after a long time of consistent work.

How many subscribers do I need to make money?

It depends on the income route. Services and products can earn with very few subscribers. Ad programmes have eligibility requirements that change, so check YouTube's current rules. Sponsorships depend on your niche and audience.

How long does it take?

Often a year or more to build a small audience and meaningful income, and some take longer. Consistent, improving videos matter more than speed.

Do I need to show my face?

No. Many successful channels use voiceovers, hands, screen recordings, text or animation. Choose what you can sustain.

What equipment do I need?

A phone, a quiet space, soft light and ideally a small microphone. Good sound and light matter more than an expensive camera.

How often should I post?

As often as you can keep up for months. For many beginners, one video a week is a good rhythm. Consistency beats intensity.

Should I make Shorts or long videos?

Both can help. Shorts can introduce you to new people. Long videos tend to build trust and serve search. Many creators use Shorts as tasters that lead to longer videos. Check current rules and monetisation details for each.

Can I use popular music?

Not unless you have the right to. Use music from sources that allow it on YouTube, and read the licence. A copyright claim can affect your videos.

Can I buy subscribers or views to get started?

Please do not. It breaks the rules, can harm your channel and does not give you real viewers.

What if I get negative comments?

Use moderation tools, block and report abusive accounts and reply only when helpful. Do not let strangers decide whether you continue.

What should I do about taxes?

Many countries expect you to report income from online sources, and YouTube may ask for tax information. Rules differ and change. I am not a tax adviser, so check official guidance and consider speaking to a qualified person.

What should I do after my first ten videos?

Review your analytics, double down on what worked, improve your hooks, choose your first income route and keep going with a sustainable rhythm.

30What To Do Next

You have reached the end of a very long guide, and that tells me something lovely about you: you are willing to learn a craft properly, not just chase views.

Here is what I want you to keep. A YouTube channel is not a lottery ticket and it is not a fairy tale. It is a body of useful work, built one video at a time, for a specific person who needs what you share. The creators who build something lasting are rarely the most polished or the most lucky. They are the ones who chose a clear niche, made videos that answered real questions, improved a little each time, built several honest income routes and stayed long enough for trust to grow.

So here is your next step, and it is small. Tonight, choose your niche and write your channel promise. Tomorrow, set up your channel and secure it. This week, plan and film your first video, even if it is imperfect. In a month, you could have three videos out and your first lessons from real viewers. In three months, you could have a rhythm, a clearer audience and your first small income route.

When it is slow, remember that slow is still moving. When a video flops, learn from it. When someone writes a kind comment, save it. And when you want to quit, take a rest, not a decision.

When you are ready for more, here are good next steps. Instagram Pays Too, Sis shows how to use another platform alongside YouTube. Personal Branding For Beginners helps people remember who you are. The Soft Girl's Guide To Passive Income shows how to build income from content that keeps working. How To Start And Grow A Profitable Digital Product Business helps you turn your knowledge into products. And our free Academy courses are a gentle place to practise.

I am rooting for you, babe. Begin tonight, go gently and keep going.
